label: Parasitology
blurb: Protozoa, nematodes, cestodes, trematodes — life cycle, disease, and drug

organisms.name: Plasmodium falciparum
organisms.labFeatures: Thick and thin blood smears show ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes with high parasitemia and all erythrocyte stages infected; no hypnozoites; rapid antigen tests
organisms.manifestations: Irregular continuous fever, cerebral malaria with seizures and coma, severe hemolytic anemia, blackwater fever, acute kidney injury, and ARDS
organisms.treatment: Intravenous artesunate for severe malaria; artemisinin-based combination therapy for uncomplicated cases; no primaquine needed since there are no hypnozoites
organisms.transmission: Bite of the female Anopheles mosquito; also congenital and transfusion-transmitted
organisms.virulenceFactor: PfEMP1 mediates erythrocyte rosetting and adhesion to endothelium causing microvascular obstruction and cerebral malaria; infects red cells of all ages
organisms.tooltip: The deadly species, because it infects red cells of every age and sequesters in capillaries. Sickle trait, G6PD deficiency, and thalassemia all confer partial protection.

organisms.name: Plasmodium vivax / ovale
organisms.labFeatures: Blood smear shows enlarged infected red cells with Schuffner dots; infects only reticulocytes so parasitemia stays low; dormant hypnozoites in the liver
organisms.manifestations: Tertian fever every 48 hours with chills and rigors, splenomegaly, mild anemia, and relapses months to years later from hepatic hypnozoites
organisms.treatment: Chloroquine or ACT for blood stages, plus primaquine or tafenoquine to eradicate hypnozoites after G6PD testing
organisms.transmission: Anopheles mosquito bite; vivax requires Duffy antigen on red cells for invasion
organisms.virulenceFactor: Hypnozoite dormancy in hepatocytes allowing relapse long after the mosquito exposure; restriction to reticulocytes limits parasite burden
organisms.tooltip: Only vivax and ovale form hypnozoites, so only they relapse and only they need primaquine. Duffy-negative individuals, common in West Africa, are resistant to vivax.

organisms.name: Babesia microti
organisms.labFeatures: Blood smear shows Maltese cross tetrads and pleomorphic ring forms within red cells; no pigment; PCR and serology; hemolytic anemia with high LDH
organisms.manifestations: Fever, drenching sweats, hemolytic anemia, and fatigue; severe or fatal disease in asplenic, elderly, or immunocompromised patients
organisms.treatment: Atovaquone plus azithromycin for mild disease; clindamycin plus quinine for severe disease; exchange transfusion for high parasitemia
organisms.transmission: Ixodes scapularis tick bite in the northeastern and upper midwestern United States; also blood transfusion; coinfection with Lyme is common
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intraerythrocytic replication causing hemolysis; the spleen is critical for clearance, which is why asplenia predicts severe disease
organisms.tooltip: Maltese cross tetrads distinguish it from malaria, as does absence of hemozoin pigment and no travel history. Ask about splenectomy — it predicts fulminant disease.

organisms.name: Toxoplasma gondii
organisms.labFeatures: Tachyzoites and tissue bradyzoite cysts on histology; serology for IgM and IgG; ring-enhancing lesions in the basal ganglia on MRI; PCR of CSF or amniotic fluid
organisms.manifestations: Asymptomatic or mononucleosis-like illness in healthy hosts; necrotizing encephalitis with multiple ring-enhancing lesions in AIDS with CD4 below 100; congenital chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications
organisms.treatment: Sulfadiazine plus pyrimethamine with leucovorin; TMP-SMX for prophylaxis when CD4 is below 100
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of oocysts from cat feces, undercooked meat containing tissue cysts, and transplacental transmission
organisms.virulenceFactor: Formation of a parasitophorous vacuole that resists lysosomal fusion; lifelong bradyzoite cysts in brain and muscle that reactivate with T-cell loss
organisms.tooltip: Congenital triad: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and intracranial calcifications — diffuse calcifications here versus periventricular in CMV. In AIDS, multiple ring-enhancing lesions versus a single lesion in CNS lymphoma.

organisms.name: Trypanosoma cruzi
organisms.labFeatures: Trypomastigotes in blood and intracellular amastigotes in tissue on Giemsa stain; serology for chronic disease; megacolon or cardiomegaly on imaging
organisms.manifestations: Acute phase with Romana sign (unilateral periorbital swelling) and chagoma; chronic Chagas disease with dilated cardiomyopathy, apical aneurysm, megaesophagus, and megacolon
organisms.treatment: Benznidazole or nifurtimox, effective mainly in acute and early chronic disease; supportive management of cardiomyopathy
organisms.transmission: Reduviid (kissing) bug feces rubbed into the bite wound or mucosa, in rural Latin America; also congenital and transfusion-related
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intracellular amastigote replication in cardiac myocytes and autonomic ganglia, with autoimmune destruction of myenteric plexus neurons
organisms.tooltip: Destruction of the myenteric plexus causes megaesophagus and megacolon, mirroring achalasia and Hirschsprung disease. Apical aneurysm with cardioembolic stroke is the cardiac signature.

organisms.name: Trypanosoma brucei
organisms.labFeatures: Trypomastigotes in blood, lymph node aspirate, or CSF on Giemsa; elevated CSF protein and IgM; Winterbottom sign with posterior cervical lymphadenopathy
organisms.manifestations: African sleeping sickness: hemolymphatic stage with intermittent fever and adenopathy, then meningoencephalitic stage with daytime somnolence, personality change, and coma
organisms.treatment: Fexinidazole orally for both stages where available; suramin or pentamidine for early stage; melarsoprol or eflornithine for CNS stage
organisms.transmission: Bite of the tsetse fly in sub-Saharan Africa; rhodesiense is zoonotic and acute, gambiense is anthroponotic and chronic
organisms.virulenceFactor: Variant surface glycoprotein antigenic variation producing recurrent waves of parasitemia that outpace antibody responses
organisms.tooltip: VSG switching causes the undulating fever curve — each antibody wave clears one variant as the next emerges. Reversal of the sleep-wake cycle gives the disease its name.

organisms.name: Leishmania species
organisms.labFeatures: Intracellular amastigotes within macrophages on Giemsa stain of bone marrow, spleen, or skin lesion; positive rK39 serology; pancytopenia in visceral disease
organisms.manifestations: Cutaneous leishmaniasis with a chronic painless ulcer and raised border; visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar) with fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and darkened skin
organisms.treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B for visceral disease; miltefosine or antimonials; topical or intralesional therapy for localized cutaneous disease
organisms.transmission: Bite of the female sandfly in the Middle East, South Asia, Africa, and Latin America; dogs and rodents serve as reservoirs
organisms.virulenceFactor: Survival and replication within macrophage phagolysosomes by inhibiting oxidative burst; lipophosphoglycan surface coat resists complement
organisms.tooltip: Kala-azar means black fever, for the skin darkening. Massive splenomegaly with pancytopenia and fever in a traveler from South Asia or East Africa should raise it.

organisms.name: Giardia lamblia
organisms.labFeatures: Pear-shaped trophozoites with four pairs of flagella and a ventral sucking disc, plus oval cysts, in stool; stool antigen or PCR; no blood or leukocytes in stool
organisms.manifestations: Prolonged foul-smelling greasy diarrhea with bloating and flatulence, lactose intolerance, fat-soluble vitamin malabsorption and weight loss; worse in IgA deficiency
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole, tinidazole, or nitazoxanide
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral through contaminated mountain streams and lakes, daycare settings, and sexual contact; cysts resist chlorination
organisms.virulenceFactor: Ventral sucking disc attaches to duodenal mucosa causing villous blunting without invasion; variant surface protein switching evades secretory IgA
organisms.tooltip: Non-invasive, so the diarrhea is steatorrheic rather than bloody and there are no fecal leukocytes. The campers' and hikers' diarrhea. IgA deficiency predisposes to chronic infection.

organisms.name: Entamoeba histolytica
organisms.labFeatures: Trophozoites with ingested erythrocytes and cysts with up to four nuclei in stool; stool antigen or PCR; flask-shaped colonic ulcers; anchovy-paste liver abscess aspirate
organisms.manifestations: Bloody dysentery with lower abdominal pain, amebic liver abscess typically in the right lobe, toxic megacolon, and ameboma
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole or tinidazole for invasive disease, followed by paromomycin or iodoquinol to clear intraluminal cysts
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral ingestion of cysts from contaminated food and water, and sexual contact; travel to endemic areas
organisms.virulenceFactor: Galactose-binding lectin for adherence, amebapores lysing host cells, and cysteine proteases degrading extracellular matrix and IgA
organisms.tooltip: Erythrophagocytosis — trophozoites with ingested red cells — distinguishes pathogenic E. histolytica from harmless E. dispar. Liver abscess aspirate looks like anchovy paste and is usually sterile.

organisms.name: Cryptosporidium parvum
organisms.labFeatures: Acid-fast oocysts on modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain of stool, or direct fluorescent antibody; oocysts resist chlorination
organisms.manifestations: Self-limited watery diarrhea in healthy hosts; severe chronic voluminous diarrhea with wasting in AIDS with CD4 below 100; biliary tract disease
organisms.treatment: Nitazoxanide; antiretroviral therapy to restore CD4 count is the definitive treatment in AIDS; aggressive rehydration
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral through contaminated municipal water and recreational swimming pools; oocysts survive standard chlorination
organisms.virulenceFactor: Intracellular but extracytoplasmic location at the apical enterocyte surface shielding it from both immune attack and luminal drugs
organisms.tooltip: Chlorine-resistant oocysts cause swimming pool and municipal water outbreaks. In AIDS it causes litres of watery stool daily, and nothing works reliably until CD4 recovers.

organisms.name: Trichomonas vaginalis
organisms.labFeatures: Motile pear-shaped trophozoite with jerky motility on wet mount, no cyst stage; vaginal pH above 4.5; strawberry cervix; NAAT most sensitive
organisms.manifestations: Frothy green-yellow malodorous vaginal discharge with pruritus and dysuria; usually asymptomatic urethritis in men; associated with preterm birth and HIV acquisition
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole or tinidazole, with treatment of all sexual partners; a single oral dose is often sufficient
organisms.transmission: Sexual contact; there is no cyst form, so it cannot survive long outside the host
organisms.virulenceFactor: Adhesins and cysteine proteases causing epithelial microulceration (the strawberry cervix), plus degradation of local antibody
organisms.tooltip: No cyst stage means obligate sexual transmission and mandatory partner treatment. Strawberry cervix plus motile trophozoites on wet mount plus pH above 4.5 is the classic picture.

organisms.name: Naegleria fowleri
organisms.labFeatures: Motile amoeboid trophozoites visible in fresh CSF wet mount; neutrophilic CSF with low glucose and high protein mimicking bacterial meningitis; PCR
organisms.manifestations: Primary amebic meningoencephalitis with abrupt headache, fever, altered mentation, and death within about a week; altered taste or smell early
organisms.treatment: Amphotericin B plus miltefosine, rifampin, and azithromycin; survival is rare despite treatment
organisms.transmission: Forceful entry of warm fresh water into the nose while swimming or diving, or from nasal irrigation with untreated tap water
organisms.virulenceFactor: Direct invasion through the olfactory neuroepithelium and cribriform plate into the frontal lobes, with amebapores causing rapid tissue destruction
organisms.tooltip: Enters through the cribriform plate from warm fresh water, so early loss of smell or taste is a clue. Nearly uniformly fatal. Never irrigate sinuses with untreated tap water.

organisms.name: Acanthamoeba species
organisms.labFeatures: Trophozoites and double-walled cysts on corneal scraping or brain biopsy; confocal microscopy of cornea; culture on non-nutrient agar with E. coli overlay
organisms.manifestations: Severe painful keratitis with a ring infiltrate in contact lens wearers; granulomatous amebic encephalitis with a subacute course in the immunocompromised
organisms.treatment: Topical polyhexamethylene biguanide or chlorhexidine with propamidine for keratitis; multidrug regimens for encephalitis with poor outcomes
organisms.transmission: Contact lenses rinsed in tap water or homemade saline; soil and water exposure; hematogenous CNS spread in immunosuppression
organisms.virulenceFactor: Mannose-binding protein adherence to corneal epithelium, cyst resistance to disinfectants, and proteases causing stromal necrosis
organisms.tooltip: Pain out of proportion to findings in a contact lens wearer who rinses with tap water. Unlike Naegleria it causes a subacute granulomatous encephalitis rather than fulminant meningoencephalitis.

organisms.name: Ascaris lumbricoides
organisms.labFeatures: Large oval eggs with thick mamillated shells in stool; adult worms up to 35 cm may be passed or seen on imaging; eosinophilia during migration
organisms.manifestations: Loffler syndrome with transient pulmonary infiltrates and eosinophilia during larval migration; intestinal or biliary obstruction with heavy worm burden; malnutrition in children
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole; pyrantel pamoate in pregnancy; surgical or endoscopic removal for obstruction
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral ingestion of eggs from soil contaminated with human feces; the most common helminth infection worldwide
organisms.virulenceFactor: Larval migration through lung tissue triggering eosinophilic inflammation; sheer worm mass causing mechanical obstruction
organisms.tooltip: Larvae penetrate the gut, travel to lungs, get coughed up and swallowed to mature — that migration explains the transient pulmonary phase with eosinophilia (Loffler syndrome).

organisms.name: Enterobius vermicularis
organisms.labFeatures: Diagnosed with the cellophane tape test applied to the perianal skin in the morning, showing characteristic flattened-sided eggs; eggs are rarely found in stool
organisms.manifestations: Intense nocturnal perianal pruritus, restless sleep and irritability in children, secondary excoriation, and occasionally vulvovaginitis
organisms.treatment: Albendazole, mebendazole, or pyrantel pamoate, repeated in two weeks; treat the whole household and wash bedding
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral autoinfection from scratching and reinfection via fingernails, bedding, and clothing; spreads readily among household members
organisms.virulenceFactor: Nocturnal migration of gravid females to the perianal skin to deposit eggs, causing pruritus that promotes autoinfection
organisms.tooltip: The pinworm. Scotch tape test, not stool O&P. Treat everyone in the house and repeat in two weeks to catch the next cycle, because autoinfection is relentless.

organisms.name: Strongyloides stercoralis
organisms.labFeatures: Rhabditiform larvae in stool (not eggs); serology; eosinophilia; larvae in sputum during hyperinfection; agar plate culture shows larval tracks
organisms.manifestations: Larva currens serpiginous rash, abdominal pain and diarrhea, Loffler-like pulmonary symptoms; hyperinfection syndrome with gram-negative sepsis when corticosteroids are given
organisms.treatment: Ivermectin is first-line; albendazole as alternative; screen and treat before starting corticosteroids or anti-TNF therapy
organisms.transmission: Filariform larvae penetrate intact skin from contaminated soil; autoinfection allows decades-long persistence without reexposure
organisms.virulenceFactor: Unique autoinfective cycle in which larvae mature within the host, enabling lifelong infection and explosive hyperinfection under immunosuppression
organisms.tooltip: The reason to screen immigrants and travelers before steroids or anti-TNF therapy. Autoinfection means infection acquired decades ago can erupt as fatal hyperinfection with gram-negative bacteremia.

organisms.name: Necator americanus / Ancylostoma duodenale
organisms.labFeatures: Thin-shelled oval eggs in stool; microcytic hypochromic anemia with low ferritin; eosinophilia; ground itch at the entry site
organisms.manifestations: Iron deficiency anemia from intestinal blood loss, growth and cognitive impairment in children, pruritic rash at larval entry, and transient pulmonary symptoms
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole, plus iron supplementation to correct the anemia
organisms.transmission: Filariform larvae in soil penetrate bare skin, usually the feet; walking barefoot in endemic tropical regions
organisms.virulenceFactor: Cutting plates or teeth that attach to intestinal mucosa plus anticoagulant secretions, producing ongoing occult blood loss
organisms.tooltip: The hookworms and the leading infectious cause of iron deficiency anemia worldwide. Barefoot soil exposure plus microcytic anemia plus eosinophilia is the triad.

organisms.name: Trichinella spiralis
organisms.labFeatures: Encysted larvae in striated muscle on biopsy; serology; marked eosinophilia with elevated creatine kinase; periorbital edema on exam
organisms.manifestations: Early diarrhea and abdominal pain, then fever with periorbital edema, myositis, splinter hemorrhages, and in severe cases myocarditis and encephalitis
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole plus corticosteroids for severe inflammatory symptoms
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked pork, bear, or wild game containing encysted larvae
organisms.virulenceFactor: Larval encystment within skeletal muscle cells, converting them into nurse cells and provoking intense eosinophilic myositis
organisms.tooltip: Periorbital edema plus myositis plus eosinophilia after eating undercooked pork or bear meat. Larvae convert muscle cells into nurse cells to sustain themselves.

organisms.name: Wuchereria bancrofti
organisms.labFeatures: Microfilariae on nocturnal blood smear (nocturnal periodicity), circulating filarial antigen test, dilated lymphatics on ultrasound with the filarial dance sign
organisms.manifestations: Recurrent lymphangitis and lymphadenitis, then elephantiasis with massive lymphedema of legs and scrotum; tropical pulmonary eosinophilia
organisms.treatment: Diethylcarbamazine, with doxycycline to kill Wolbachia endosymbionts; ivermectin plus albendazole in areas with onchocerciasis coinfection; limb hygiene for lymphedema
organisms.transmission: Bite of Culex, Anopheles, or Aedes mosquitoes in tropical regions; requires repeated bites over years to establish heavy infection
organisms.virulenceFactor: Adult worms obstruct and damage lymphatic vessels; Wolbachia endosymbiont bacteria drive much of the inflammatory response
organisms.tooltip: Blood must be drawn at night to catch the microfilariae. Doxycycline works by killing the Wolbachia endosymbiont the worm depends on — an unusual and heavily tested mechanism.

organisms.name: Onchocerca volvulus
organisms.labFeatures: Microfilariae on skin snip (not blood), subcutaneous nodules containing adult worms, slit-lamp exam showing microfilariae in the anterior chamber; Mazzotti reaction historically
organisms.manifestations: River blindness with keratitis and sclerosing chorioretinitis, intensely pruritic dermatitis, leopard skin depigmentation, hanging groin, and onchocercomas
organisms.treatment: Ivermectin every 6 to 12 months to kill microfilariae, plus doxycycline to target Wolbachia; diethylcarbamazine is contraindicated because it can cause blindness
organisms.transmission: Bite of the Simulium blackfly, which breeds in fast-flowing rivers in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America
organisms.virulenceFactor: Microfilarial death in the eye and skin releases Wolbachia antigens that trigger the inflammation causing blindness and dermatitis
organisms.tooltip: Blackfly, fast-flowing rivers, blindness. Skin snip rather than blood smear. Diethylcarbamazine is dangerous here because rapid microfilarial killing in the eye worsens vision.

organisms.name: Loa loa
organisms.labFeatures: Microfilariae on daytime blood smear (diurnal periodicity); adult worm visible crossing the subconjunctiva; marked eosinophilia
organisms.manifestations: Calabar swellings — transient painful subcutaneous swellings on the extremities — and the adult worm visibly migrating across the conjunctiva
organisms.treatment: Diethylcarbamazine or albendazole; must exclude high microfilarial load first because rapid killing causes encephalopathy
organisms.transmission: Bite of the Chrysops deerfly or mango fly in the rainforests of West and Central Africa
organisms.virulenceFactor: Adult worm migration through subcutaneous tissue and across the eye; high microfilaremia creates risk of fatal encephalopathy with treatment
organisms.tooltip: The eye worm. Critically, ivermectin given for onchocerciasis in a Loa loa coinfected patient can cause fatal encephalopathy, which is why Loa loa burden must be assessed first.

organisms.name: Taenia solium
organisms.labFeatures: Proglottids and eggs in stool for intestinal infection; cystic brain lesions with scolex on MRI and serology for neurocysticercosis; eosinophilia variable
organisms.manifestations: Intestinal taeniasis that is often asymptomatic; neurocysticercosis with new-onset seizures from calcified or active brain cysts, hydrocephalus, and raised intracranial pressure
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel or niclosamide for intestinal tapeworm; albendazole with corticosteroids and antiepileptics for neurocysticercosis; never treat ocular cysts with antiparasitics
organisms.transmission: Undercooked pork containing cysticerci causes intestinal tapeworm; ingestion of eggs from human feces causes cysticercosis, including by autoinfection
organisms.virulenceFactor: Larval cysts evade immunity while intact; inflammation on cyst death produces the seizures, which is why treatment must be covered with steroids
organisms.tooltip: Eating the pork gives you a tapeworm; eating the eggs gives you cysticercosis. Steroids and antiepileptics come before albendazole, since dying cysts provoke the seizures.

organisms.name: Taenia saginata
organisms.labFeatures: Gravid proglottids and eggs in stool; scolex has four suckers without hooks, distinguishing it from T. solium; mild or absent eosinophilia
organisms.manifestations: Usually asymptomatic; mild abdominal discomfort, and patients may notice motile proglottids in stool or underwear
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel single dose, or niclosamide
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked beef containing cysticerci; humans are the only definitive host
organisms.virulenceFactor: Attachment via suckers to the small bowel with competition for nutrients; it does not cause cysticercosis in humans
organisms.tooltip: The beef tapeworm and the benign one — it cannot cause cysticercosis because humans do not serve as its intermediate host. Scolex has suckers but no hooks.

organisms.name: Echinococcus granulosus
organisms.labFeatures: Hepatic or pulmonary cysts with eggshell calcification and daughter cysts on imaging; serology; hydatid sand with protoscolices in aspirate
organisms.manifestations: Slowly enlarging hepatic or pulmonary hydatid cysts causing pain; anaphylaxis if a cyst ruptures; biliary obstruction
organisms.treatment: Albendazole with PAIR (puncture, aspiration, injection, reaspiration) or surgical removal with great care to avoid spillage
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of eggs from dog feces; sheep are the intermediate host, so sheep-herding regions are endemic
organisms.virulenceFactor: Highly antigenic cyst fluid that provokes anaphylaxis on spillage, and daughter cyst formation that seeds new lesions
organisms.tooltip: Never aspirate blindly — cyst rupture spills antigenic fluid and causes anaphylaxis plus dissemination. Dogs and sheep are the exposure clue; albendazole is given before and after intervention.

organisms.name: Diphyllobothrium latum
organisms.labFeatures: Operculated eggs in stool; the longest human tapeworm at up to 10 meters; macrocytic anemia with low vitamin B12 and elevated methylmalonic acid
organisms.manifestations: Often asymptomatic; vitamin B12 deficiency with megaloblastic anemia and subacute combined degeneration; abdominal discomfort
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel or niclosamide, plus vitamin B12 repletion
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of raw or undercooked freshwater fish such as salmon and pike; sushi and ceviche in endemic lake regions
organisms.virulenceFactor: Avid competition for dietary vitamin B12 in the proximal small bowel, depleting the host over time
organisms.tooltip: The fish tapeworm that steals B12, producing megaloblastic anemia with neurologic signs. Raw freshwater fish is the exposure — a useful contrast with Anisakis, which causes acute gastric pain.

organisms.name: Schistosoma mansoni / japonicum
organisms.labFeatures: Eggs with a lateral spine (mansoni) or small lateral knob (japonicum) in stool; eosinophilia; periportal pipestem fibrosis on ultrasound
organisms.manifestations: Katayama fever during acute infection; chronic hepatic periportal fibrosis with portal hypertension, variceal bleeding, and splenomegaly while liver function is preserved
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel, repeated after several weeks; corticosteroids for Katayama fever
organisms.transmission: Free-swimming cercariae from freshwater snails penetrate intact skin during wading or swimming in Africa, South America, and Asia
organisms.virulenceFactor: Egg deposition in portal venules triggering granulomatous fibrosis; adult worms coat themselves in host antigens to evade immunity
organisms.tooltip: Portal hypertension with preserved hepatocellular function — the fibrosis is periportal, not cirrhotic. Swimmer's itch and freshwater snail exposure are the clues.

organisms.name: Schistosoma haematobium
organisms.labFeatures: Eggs with a terminal spine in urine rather than stool; hematuria; bladder wall calcification on imaging; eosinophilia
organisms.manifestations: Painless terminal hematuria, chronic cystitis with bladder fibrosis, obstructive uropathy and hydronephrosis, and squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel; urologic surveillance for bladder malignancy in long-standing infection
organisms.transmission: Cercariae from freshwater snails penetrate skin during contact with fresh water in Africa and the Middle East, including the Nile
organisms.virulenceFactor: Egg deposition in the bladder venous plexus causing chronic granulomatous inflammation that drives squamous metaplasia and malignant transformation
organisms.tooltip: The only common cause of squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, which is otherwise transitional cell. Terminal-spined eggs in urine; mansoni has lateral spines in stool.

organisms.name: Clonorchis sinensis
organisms.labFeatures: Small operculated eggs in stool; biliary dilatation on imaging; eosinophilia; elevated alkaline phosphatase
organisms.manifestations: Biliary obstruction, recurrent pyogenic cholangitis, pigmented gallstones, and cholangiocarcinoma with chronic infection
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel or albendazole; ERCP for biliary obstruction
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of raw or undercooked freshwater fish in East and Southeast Asia
organisms.virulenceFactor: Adult flukes inhabit bile ducts causing chronic inflammation, epithelial hyperplasia, and periductal fibrosis that promotes malignancy
organisms.tooltip: Chronic biliary inflammation makes this a recognized cause of cholangiocarcinoma. Raw freshwater fish in East Asia plus biliary symptoms plus eosinophilia points here.

organisms.name: Paragonimus westermani
organisms.labFeatures: Operculated eggs in sputum or stool; chest imaging with cysts and ring shadows that can mimic tuberculosis; eosinophilia and pleural effusion
organisms.manifestations: Chronic cough with hemoptysis and brown-flecked sputum, pleural effusion, and sometimes cerebral involvement with seizures
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel or triclabendazole
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked freshwater crab or crayfish in East Asia, West Africa, and parts of Latin America
organisms.virulenceFactor: Larval migration through the diaphragm into lung parenchyma, forming fibrous capsules communicating with bronchioles
organisms.tooltip: A great tuberculosis mimic: chronic cough, hemoptysis, and cavitary lung lesions — but with eosinophilia and a history of undercooked crab or crayfish.

organisms.name: Sarcoptes scabiei
organisms.labFeatures: Skin scraping with mineral oil shows mites, eggs, or scybala (feces); dermoscopy shows the delta-wing jet sign; burrows in finger webs and flexor wrists
organisms.manifestations: Intensely pruritic papules worst at night in finger webs, wrists, axillae, and genitals; crusted (Norwegian) scabies with thick hyperkeratotic plaques in the immunocompromised
organisms.treatment: Topical permethrin 5% repeated in one week, or oral ivermectin; treat all household contacts and wash bedding in hot water
organisms.transmission: Prolonged skin-to-skin contact, including sexual contact; fomites matter mainly in crusted scabies with its huge mite burden
organisms.virulenceFactor: Burrowing into the stratum corneum with a delayed type IV hypersensitivity response to mite antigen causing the pruritus
organisms.tooltip: Itching reflects hypersensitivity, so it begins weeks after infestation and persists for weeks after successful treatment. Crusted scabies carries thousands of mites and is highly contagious.

organisms.name: Pediculus humanus
organisms.labFeatures: Visual identification of adult lice and nits cemented to hair shafts; wet combing increases detection; nits within 1 cm of the scalp suggest active infestation
organisms.manifestations: Scalp or body pruritus with excoriation and secondary bacterial infection; body lice can transmit epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, and trench fever
organisms.treatment: Permethrin or dimethicone for head lice with repeat application; wet combing; body lice resolve with bathing and laundering clothes
organisms.transmission: Head-to-head contact and shared combs or hats for head lice; crowded unhygienic conditions and infested clothing for body lice
organisms.virulenceFactor: Saliva-induced hypersensitivity causing pruritus; body lice act as vectors for Rickettsia prowazekii, Borrelia recurrentis, and Bartonella quintana
organisms.tooltip: Head lice are a nuisance; body lice are a vector, carrying epidemic typhus, relapsing fever, and trench fever — which is why delousing matters in refugee and wartime settings.
